Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(InStyle.com) -- It takes a truly adventurous actress to pull off a razored Mohawk, a platinum pixie and a Louise Brooks bob, but we'd expect nothing less from the ever provocative Selma Blair, who experimented with all three looks in under a year. Selma Blair says she works with hairstylists and makeup artists who "have a vision." "I have no fears when it comes to my hair or clothes," proclaims the 36-year-old star of NBC's upcoming mom-and-daughter sitcom "Kath and Kim" and July's action flick "Hellboy II: The Golden Army." Makeup, however, is an entirely different matter for the self-declared "poor applier," who sticks with basics like nude lipstick and pink blush, and ducks whenever she sees a liquid liner. "I avoid anything difficult," she says. Blair's signature look: "A rosy cheek, a smudgy eye, a lot of mascara--I look like a doll that has too much makeup on, and I love it!" Have you always been a beauty chameleon? In high school I would mess with my hair and makeup all the time. I used to wear a shirt that said "Ms. Clairol" because I changed my hair color so much. I was blond for a long time, then what my mom called "barnyard red." Do you still dye it yourself? Only when I have to cover up stray grays. And I'll just use whatever color I find in the grocery store that looks good on the box, like Preference by L'Oréal--because I'm worth it [laughs]. But for my platinum hair, I went to Sheri at Román Salon in L.A. She was a saint. I had just dyed my hair dark brown, so she had to very slowly strip out all the color so that my hair wouldn't burn off. And the cut--are you keeping it short? I tend to like my hair whatever way it's not, so now I miss it being long. I think I'm more approachable with long hair. When it's short, I come across as being artsy and weird. What's your typical makeup look? I used to wear a lot of red lipstick, and when I got a pimple, I'd cover it up with eyeliner to turn it into a beauty mark. But everything has changed since I hit 35. I'm at an age where any makeup that's meant to look "slept in" really looks like I slept in it. That's for youngsters! Now less is more. I don't like to wear concealer or anything. I'd rather have uneven skin than feel like my face is cracking from too much foundation. Then you must be serious about your skin care. I go to a spa in L.A. called Kinara for its Skin Care BootCamp. You go once a week for 12 sessions and they'll look at your skin and tell you how to get it in better condition. They really helped me a lot. I also stay out of the sun. Any thoughts on Botox or plastic surgery? I wanted to get Botox once to make me feel younger. But I don't really have [enough wrinkles] to justify it yet. As for going under the knife, I can't say I wouldn't, but I haven't thought too much about it. Best beauty product? Egyptian Magic cream is my saving grace for everything. It works for my friend's baby's bottom, and I can also use it instead of Chapstick. So what's next? I'm really excited about having a perma-tan and wearing long highlighted hair extensions for my role on "Kath and Kim." And I've been gaining weight for the part by eating a little bit more of what I want and not moving around as much. I've already put on 15 pounds, and I'll probably gain another 10. It'll be a whole new me! Will this be your most drastic transformation? Actually I wore huge prosthetic boobs for a John Waters movie. They were glued on every day by a really handsome guy, but ripping them off every night was definitely outside my realm of comfort. After those bosoms, I didn't mind being flat-chested anymore! (InStyle.com) -- It takes a truly adventurous actress to pull off a razored Mohawk, a platinum pixie, and a Louise Brooks bob, but we would expect nothing less from the ever-provocative Selma Blair, who experimented with all three looks within a single year. Blair credits her hairstylists and makeup artists with having "a vision." "I have no fears when it comes to my hair or clothes," proclaims the 36-year-old star of NBC's upcoming mother-daughter sitcom "Kath and Kim" and July's action film "Hellboy II: The Golden Army." Makeup, however, is an entirely different matter for the self-declared "poor applier," who sticks to basics like nude lipstick and pink blush, and shies away at the mere sight of liquid liner. "I avoid anything difficult," she admits. Blair describes her signature look as "a rosy cheek, a smudged eye, and plenty of mascara—I look like a doll wearing too much makeup, and I love it!"

**Have you always been a beauty chameleon?**
In high school, I was constantly experimenting with my hair and makeup. I used to wear a shirt that read "Ms. Clairol" because I changed my hair color so frequently. I was blond for a long stretch, then what my mother called "barnyard red."

**Do you still dye it yourself?**
Only when I need to cover stray grays. I'll simply grab whatever color catches my eye on a box at the grocery store—Preference by L'Oréal, say—because I'm worth it [laughs]. But for my platinum look, I went to Sheri at Román Salon in L.A. She was an absolute saint. I had just dyed my hair dark brown, so she had to carefully strip out the color, layer by layer, to keep my hair from burning.

**And the cut—are you keeping it short?**
I tend to want whatever my hair currently isn't, so at the moment, I miss having it long. I think I come across as more approachable with long hair. When it's short, people read me as artsy and a bit eccentric.

**What's your typical makeup look?**
I used to wear a lot of red lipstick, and if I got a pimple, I'd disguise it with eyeliner and pass it off as a beauty mark. But everything changed once I turned 35. At this age, any makeup meant to look "just rolled out of bed" genuinely looks like I just rolled out of bed. That effect is for the young! Now, less is more. I steer clear of concealer and similar products—I'd rather live with uneven skin than feel like my face is cracking under too much foundation.

**Then you must take skin care seriously.**
I visit a spa in L.A. called Kinara for its Skin Care Boot Camp. You attend weekly for twelve sessions, and they assess your skin and advise you on how to improve its condition. It's made a real difference for me. I also make a point of staying out of the sun.

**Any thoughts on Botox or plastic surgery?**
I once considered Botox to feel a bit younger, but honestly, I don't have enough wrinkles yet to justify it. As for surgery, I wouldn't rule it out, but it's not something I've given much thought to.

**Best beauty product?**
Egyptian Magic cream is my saving grace for absolutely everything. It works wonders on my friend's baby's bottom, and I also use it in place of Chapstick.

**So what's next?**
I'm genuinely excited about sporting a permanent tan and long, highlighted hair extensions for my role on "Kath and Kim." I've also been gaining weight for the part—eating a bit more of what I crave and staying less active. I've already put on fifteen pounds, and I expect to gain another ten. It'll be a whole new me!

**Will this be your most drastic transformation?**
Actually, I once wore enormous prosthetic breasts for a John Waters film. They were glued on each morning by a remarkably handsome man, but peeling them off every night was well outside my comfort zone. After that experience, being flat-chested never bothered me again!

**Selma Blair: Fearless with Hair, Cautious with Cosmetics**

(InStyle.com) -- Only a genuinely bold performer could carry off a shaved-sides Mohawk, an icy-blonde pixie cut, and a Louise Brooks-inspired bob—all within a single year's span. Yet this is exactly what fans have come to expect from Selma Blair, whose willingness to experiment knows no bounds. The actress credits her collaborators, noting that the hairstylists and makeup professionals she works with "have a vision."

"When it comes to hair or wardrobe, nothing scares me," declares the 36-year-old, who stars in NBC's forthcoming sitcom about a mother-daughter duo, "Kath and Kim," and appears in this July's "Hellboy II: The Golden Army."

Cosmetics, though, present a different challenge entirely. Blair, who admits she's not skilled at applying makeup, gravitates toward simple choices—a nude lip, a touch of pink on the cheeks—and steers clear entirely of liquid eyeliner. "Anything complicated, I just avoid," she explains. Her go-to appearance? "Rosy cheeks, smudged eyes, tons of mascara—it makes me look like an overly made-up doll, and honestly, I'm into it."

**Has transforming your look always come naturally to you?**
Back in high school, I constantly played around with my hair and makeup. I even owned a shirt reading "Ms. Clairol" because I switched hair colors so often. There was a long blonde phase, followed by what my mother referred to as "barnyard red."

**Do you handle the dyeing yourself these days?**
Only for touching up gray hairs here and there. I grab whatever box looks appealing at the supermarket—Preference by L'Oréal usually, because, well, I'm worth it [laughs]. The platinum look, however, required a professional—Sheri, over at Román Salon in Los Angeles. She was incredibly patient, since my hair had just been dyed dark brown and she had to gradually lift out the color to prevent damage.

**Will you stick with the shorter cut?**
Funny enough, I always crave whatever style I don't currently have—so now I'm missing long hair. With longer locks, I feel like people find me more approachable. Short hair gives off more of an artsy, quirky vibe.

**Describe your usual makeup routine.**
There was a time I loved bold red lips, and if a blemish popped up, I'd disguise it with eyeliner, turning it into a fake beauty mark. Everything shifted once I turned 35, though. At this stage in life, that "just rolled out of bed" makeup look actually just looks like I rolled out of bed—that's a trend better suited to younger women. These days, minimal is my mantra. I skip concealer entirely; I'd rather show uneven skin than feel weighed down by heavy foundation.

**You must prioritize skincare, then.**
I visit a Los Angeles spa called Kinara for their Skin Care BootCamp program—twelve weekly sessions where they assess your skin and offer guidance on improving it. It's made a real difference. Beyond that, I simply avoid sun exposure.

**Have you considered Botox or cosmetic surgery?**
I once thought about trying Botox just to feel more youthful, but honestly, I don't have enough wrinkles yet to warrant it. Surgery isn't off the table completely, but it's not something I've spent much time contemplating.

**Favorite beauty product?**
Egyptian Magic cream saves me constantly—it's incredibly versatile. My friend even uses it on her baby's skin, and I swap it in for lip balm regularly.

**What's coming up for you?**
I'm looking forward to sporting a permanent tan and long extensions with highlights for my "Kath and Kim" character. I've also been putting on weight for the role—eating more freely and cutting back on exercise. I've gained 15 pounds already and expect to add roughly 10 more. It's going to be quite the transformation!

**Will this be the biggest physical change you've undergone for a role?**
Actually, no—that title goes to a John Waters film where I wore massive prosthetic breasts. A very attractive makeup artist would glue them on each morning, but peeling them off nightly was genuinely uncomfortable. After that experience, being flat-chested felt like a relief!

# Selma Blair's Fearless Approach to Beauty and Self-Expression

Selma Blair has built a reputation as one of Hollywood's most daring beauty chameleons, unafraid to take risks that would make many actresses hesitant, particularly when it comes to hair. In a single remarkable year, she cycled through an astonishing range of looks—from an edgy, razored Mohawk to a sleek platinum pixie cut, and finally to a sophisticated Louise Brooks-inspired bob. This willingness to dramatically transform her appearance speaks to a woman who views her hair not as something to be precious about, but as a canvas for creative expression and reinvention.

Interestingly, this boldness doesn't extend to every aspect of her beauty routine. While Blair exudes confidence when it comes to hair and clothing experimentation, she's remarkably candid about her limitations elsewhere. She openly admits to being a "poor applier" of makeup, steering clear of technically demanding looks like precise liquid eyeliner application. This self-awareness reveals an authenticity that sets her apart—she's not interested in perfecting every skill, only in embracing what feels natural and achievable for her.

Instead, Blair has cultivated a signature makeup aesthetic that plays to her strengths: rosy, flushed cheeks, deliberately smudgy eye makeup, and generous, heavy mascara. She herself describes this look with characteristic wit, comparing it to a doll wearing too much makeup—an image that's both self-deprecating and oddly charming, capturing the slightly imperfect, lived-in quality of her go-to style.

This penchant for experimentation isn't a recent development but traces back to her high school years, when her hair color changed so frequently that she once wore a shirt emblazoned with "Ms. Clairol" as a playful nod to her ever-evolving look. That spirit of DIY transformation persists today; rather than relying on professional colorists, Blair still dyes her own hair using simple drugstore products, primarily to keep her grays at bay—a practical approach that mirrors her down-to-earth attitude toward beauty.

Beyond aesthetics, Blair has also reflected on how her hair length shapes not just her appearance but how others perceive her. She's noted that when her hair is short, she comes across as "artsy and weird," embodying a more unconventional, creative energy. Conversely, longer hair shifts her self-perception toward feeling more approachable and accessible. This awareness highlights how deeply intertwined hair can be with identity and social perception—for Blair, it's not merely about style, but about the different versions of herself she can inhabit through these transformations.

# Selma Blair Gets Real About Beauty, Aging, and Embracing Change

*This article was originally published on InStyle.com and appears here through a content partnership.*

---

Selma Blair has never been one to shy away from authenticity—whether discussing her health journey or her ever-evolving relationship with beauty. The actress, known for her roles in "Cruel Intentions" and "Legally Blonde," sat down with InStyle to talk about her recent hair transformations, her refreshingly simple approach to makeup, and the skincare philosophy that keeps her glowing.

**INSTYLE: You've had so many different hair looks over the years—from long blonde waves to a buzz cut. What's your relationship with your hair like these days?**

SELMA BLAIR: It's been a journey, honestly. My hair has become this symbol of transformation for me. When I shaved my head, it was freeing in a way I didn't expect. Now that it's growing back, I'm having fun with it—embracing the texture, the shorter length. I used to be so attached to having "the right hair," and now I just think, this is what's growing out of my head today, and that's kind of beautiful.

**INSTYLE: Do you have a go-to hairstylist or product you swear by?**

BLAIR: I love a good texturizing spray—it makes second-day hair actually look intentional. And I'm not precious about it anymore. Some days it's slicked back, some days it's wild. I've stopped trying to control it so much.

**INSTYLE: Let's talk makeup. What does your everyday routine look like?**

BLAIR: Minimal, honestly. I'm a big believer in a good tinted moisturizer or light foundation, cream blush—I dab it on with my fingers—and mascara. If I'm feeling fancy, a red lip. I don't love a full face every day. I want to look like myself, just a little more awake.

**INSTYLE: Any products you consider holy grails?**

BLAIR: A good concealer is non-negotiable. And I love a lip balm with a tint—something I can swipe on without a mirror. I'm not big on elaborate routines when it comes to makeup. I'd rather spend that time on skincare, honestly.

**INSTYLE: Speaking of skincare, what does that routine look like?**

BLAIR: I keep it pretty simple but consistent. Gentle cleanser, a good moisturizer, SPF always—non-negotiable. I've become much more diligent about sunscreen as I've gotten older. At night, I like a nourishing oil or a richer cream. I've learned to listen to my skin—some days it wants more hydration, some days less.

**INSTYLE: Has your approach to beauty changed as you've navigated health challenges?**

BLAIR: Completely. I used to think beauty was about achieving some kind of perfection. Now I see it as an extension of taking care of myself—of self-respect, really. Some days getting dressed and putting on a little makeup is an act of joy, not obligation. I've let go of a lot of the pressure I used to put on myself.

**INSTYLE: Any beauty advice you'd give your younger self?**

BLAIR: Stop picking yourself apart. You're going to look back at pictures of yourself at 25 and think, "I was gorgeous—why didn't I know that?" So maybe just try to enjoy it a little more now.

---

*For more exclusive celebrity interviews, visit InStyle.com.*

*The following is a fictional interview created for creative/entertainment purposes.*

---

**Interviewer:** Selma, thank you for sitting down with us. I have to start with the hair—you've had everything from a mohawk to a pixie to a bob. What draws you to switching it up so dramatically?

**Selma Blair:** Honestly, I get bored! [laughs] But it's deeper than that too. My hair has become this really personal marker of where I am in my life. When I shaved the sides for the mohawk phase, that was me feeling rebellious, wanting to reclaim something. The pixie came later—it felt more grounded, almost like a return to simplicity after some hard years. And the bob is just... chic ease. Some days you want to make a statement, some days you want to walk out the door and feel put together without much effort.

**Interviewer:** Does your health journey factor into those choices at all?

**Selma Blair:** Absolutely. When you've dealt with MS and all the physical unpredictability that comes with it, hair becomes one of the few things you can control. Cutting it short was liberating in a way I didn't expect. There's something almost ceremonial about it—shedding a version of yourself.

**Interviewer:** Let's talk beauty routine. What are your go-to makeup products these days?

**Selma Blair:** I've become such a minimalist! I love a good tinted moisturizer—something with skincare benefits built in because my skin needs the extra love these days. A cream blush I can blend with my fingers, always. I'm not big on precision anymore; I want things I can apply quickly, sitting down if I need to. A great brow gel is non-negotiable, and then a bold lip—usually a red or a deep berry—because that's the one thing that makes me feel instantly "done," even if everything else is bare.

**Interviewer:** Very chic. Now, the exciting part—tell us about joining the cast of "Kath and Kim"!

**Selma Blair:** [laughs] I'm so thrilled about this! It's such an iconic property, and stepping into that world feels like a joy bomb after some heavier years. I can't reveal too much about the character, but I will say she's got a real spark—a little unhinged, very funny, and not afraid to embarrass herself for a laugh. **Interviewer:** Comedy feels like a shift for you.

**Selma Blair:** It is, but it's also coming home in a way. I started in comedies, and there's something so healing about making people laugh. After everything, I wanted joy in my work again. This role feels like exactly that.

**Interviewer:** We cannot wait to see it. Thank you, Selma.

**Selma Blair:** Thank you! This was fun.

# Selma Blair's Beauty Revolution: Grace, Grit, and Getting Real

There's a particular kind of radiance that comes from someone who has stopped performing for the camera and started living for herself. Selma Blair has that radiance in spades. Sitting across from her—effortlessly chic in a cream cashmere sweater, her signature dark hair catching the afternoon light—it's clear that beauty, for her, has become less about perfection and more about presence.

## A New Relationship With the Mirror

"I used to obsess over every detail," Blair admits, laughing softly. "Now I look in the mirror and I'm just grateful I get to see myself at all." Since her multiple sclerosis diagnosis became public in 2018, Blair's relationship with her appearance has transformed into something deeper—a practice of self-compassion rather than self-criticism.

"Beauty isn't about hiding what's happening in your body. It's about honoring it," she says. That philosophy now guides everything from her skincare routine to her approach to aging.

## The Skincare Secrets Worth Stealing

Blair's regimen is refreshingly uncomplicated. "I'm a big believer in consistency over complexity," she explains. Her non-negotiables include:

- **A gentle, hydrating cleanser** — "I stopped stripping my skin years ago. Softness is the goal now."
- **Facial oils** — "Rosehip and marula oil are in constant rotation. My skin drinks them up."
- **SPF, religiously** — "No exceptions, even when I'm not leaving the house."
- **Cold jade rollers** — "It's part ritual, part meditation. It calms my nervous system as much as my skin."

She's also candid about the role rest and nutrition play. "Sleep is the real miracle serum. I used to burn the candle at both ends. Not anymore."

## On Botox: Honesty Over Perfection

When the conversation turns to injectables, Blair doesn't dodge the question. "I've done Botox, sure. I'm not precious about it," she says with characteristic candor. "But I also don't chase an erased face. I want to still look like *me*—someone who's laughed, cried, lived."
